title: Part 2, Chapter 38
paragraphs: In which the Distressed Duenna tells the story of her misfortunes

After the mournful musicians, as many as twelve duennas filed into the garden in two lines, all wearing wide mourning habits that looked like milled serge, with hoods of fine white gauze so long that only the hem of the robe showed beneath them. Behind them came the Countess Trifaldi, led by the hand by the squire Trifaldin of the White Beard. She was dressed in the finest unnapped black baize — so fine that, had it carried a nap, every tuft would have stood out as big as a Martos chickpea. Her train, or skirt, or whatever the thing ought to be called, ended in three points, each held aloft by the hands of a page, the three pages dressed in mourning as well, so that the three acute angles formed by the three points made an elegant geometrical figure. Everyone who saw the peaked skirt concluded that it must be the reason the countess was called Trifaldi — as if to say, Countess of the Three Skirts — and Benengeli confirms it, adding that her real name was Countess Lobuna, because wolves bred in great numbers in her country; if they had been foxes instead of wolves, she would have been called Countess Zorruna, since it was the custom in those parts for lords to take their distinctive titles from whatever thing or things were most plentiful in their lands. This countess, however, in honor of the new fashion of her skirt, dropped Lobuna and took up Trifaldi.

The twelve duennas and their lady advanced at a processional pace, their faces covered with black veils — not transparent ones like Trifaldin’s, but woven so closely that nothing at all could be seen through them. The moment the company of duennas came fully into view, the duke, the duchess, and Don Quixote rose to their feet, as did everyone else watching the slow-moving procession. The twelve duennas halted and formed a lane, and down it came the Distressed One, with Trifaldin still holding her hand. Seeing this, the duke, the duchess, and Don Quixote walked some twelve paces forward to receive her. Then, kneeling on the ground, she spoke in a voice more hoarse and rough than fine and delicate: “May it please your highnesses not to lavish such courtesies on this your servant — I should say this your handmaid — for I am in such distress that I shall never manage to make a fitting reply, since my strange and unheard-of misfortune has carried off my wits to I know not where; it must be somewhere very far away, because the more I search for them, the less of them I find.”

“The man who failed to see your worth in your very person, señora countess,” said the duke, “would be the one short of wits, for a single glance shows you deserve all the cream of courtesy and the flower of fine breeding.” And raising her by the hand, he led her to a seat beside the duchess, who welcomed her with equal graciousness. Don Quixote kept silent, while Sancho was dying to see the face of Trifaldi and one or two of her many duennas; but there was no chance of that until they chose to unveil themselves of their own accord and free will.

Everyone kept still, waiting to see who would break the silence, and it was the Distressed Duenna who did, in these words: “I am confident, most mighty lord, most beautiful lady, and most discerning company, that my most miserable misery will find in your most valiant breasts a reception no less calm than generous and compassionate, for it is misery enough to melt marble, soften diamonds, and bend the steel of the hardest hearts in the world. But before it is published to your hearing — not to say your ears — I should like to be told whether there is present in this society, circle, or company that knight immaculatissimus, Don Quixote de la Manchissima, and his squirissimus Panza.”

“The Panza is here,” said Sancho before anyone else could answer, “and Don Quixotissimus too; so, most distressedest Duenissima, you may say whatever you wishissimus, for we are all entirely readissimus to do you any servissimus.”

At this Don Quixote rose and addressed the Distressed Duenna: “If your sorrows, afflicted lady, can promise themselves any hope of relief from the valor or strength of any knight-errant, here are mine, which, feeble and limited though they are, shall be devoted entirely to your service. I am Don Quixote of La Mancha, whose calling it is to come to the aid of the needy of every kind; and that being so, señora, you have no need to appeal to anyone’s goodwill or work through preambles — simply tell your troubles plainly and directly, for you are speaking to listeners who will know how to sympathize with them even if they cannot remedy them.”

When she heard this, the Distressed Duenna made as if to throw herself at Don Quixote’s feet — and in fact she did fall before them, and said, struggling to embrace them, “Before these feet and these legs I cast myself, O unconquered knight, for they are what they are: the foundations and pillars of knight-errantry. These feet I long to kiss, for upon their steps hangs and depends the only remedy for my misfortune, O valorous errant, whose true achievements leave behind and eclipse the fabled ones of the Amadises, the Esplandians, and the Belianises!” Then, turning from Don Quixote to Sancho Panza and seizing his hands, she said, “O you, the most loyal squire that ever served a knight-errant in this present age or in ages past, whose goodness stretches further than the beard of my companion Trifaldin here present, well may you boast that in serving the great Don Quixote you are serving, gathered into one, the whole host of knights that have ever borne arms in this world. I implore you, by what you owe to your most loyal goodness, to be my kind intercessor with your master, so that he may swiftly come to the aid of this most humble and most unfortunate countess.”

To this Sancho answered, “As for my goodness, señora, being as long and as great as your squire’s beard — that matters very little to me. May my soul be well bearded and mustached when it comes time to leave this life; that is what counts. About beards down here I care little or nothing. But without all these blandishments and pleadings, I will ask my master — for I know he loves me, and besides, he needs me just now for a certain piece of business — to help and favor your worship as far as he can. So unpack your woes and lay them out before us, and leave the rest to us, for we shall all be of one mind.”

The duke and duchess, who had set up this whole adventure themselves, were ready to burst with laughter at all of it, and between themselves they praised how cleverly the Trifaldi played her part. Returning to her seat, she said, “Over the famous kingdom of Kandy, which lies between the great Trapobana and the Southern Sea, two leagues beyond Cape Comorin, reigned Queen Doña Maguncia, widow of King Archipiela, her lord and husband. From their marriage came the Princess Antonomasia, heiress to the kingdom, and this Princess Antonomasia was raised and educated under my care and direction, since I was the oldest and highest-ranking of her mother’s duennas. Time went by, and young Antonomasia reached the age of fourteen with such perfect beauty that nature could not have raised it higher. Nor should anyone suppose her mind was a child’s: she was as intelligent as she was beautiful, and she was more beautiful than anyone in the world — and still is, unless the envious fates and the three hard-hearted sisters have cut her thread of life. They have not, though, for Heaven would never allow so great a wrong to Earth as plucking, unripe, the grapes of the loveliest vineyard on its surface. Countless princes, not only of her own country but of others, fell in love with this beauty, to which my poor feeble tongue cannot do justice; and among them a private gentleman at the court dared to lift his thoughts to the heaven of such loveliness, trusting in his youth, his gallant bearing, his many talents and graces, and his quick and ready wit. For I may tell your highnesses, if it does not weary you, that he played the guitar so that it fairly spoke; he was a poet besides, and a fine dancer; and he could build birdcages so well that he might have earned his living by making them alone, had he ever been reduced to utter poverty — and gifts and graces of that kind are enough to bring down a mountain, never mind a tender young girl. But all his gallantry, wit, and gaiety, all his talents and accomplishments, would have done him little or no good toward taking the fortress of my pupil if the shameless thief had not first taken the precaution of capturing me. First the villain, the heartless vagabond, set out to win my goodwill and buy my consent, so that I, like a treacherous gatekeeper, would hand him the keys of the fortress I was set to guard. In short, he worked his way into my mind and broke down my resolve with I know not what trinkets and jewels he gave me; but what made me give way more than anything else, what brought about my fall, was some verses I heard him singing one night from a grated window that opened onto the street where he lived. If I remember rightly, they ran like this:

From that sweet enemy of mine
my bleeding heart has taken its wound;
and to make the torment greater, I am bound
to suffer it and give no sign.

The lines seemed pearls to me, and his voice sweet as syrup; and afterwards — indeed ever since, looking at the misfortune I fell into through them — I have thought that poets ought to be banished from all well-governed states, as Plato advised: at least the love poets, for they write verses not like those of ‘The Marquis of Mantua,’ which delight women and children and draw their tears, but sharp-pointed conceits that pierce the heart like soft thorns and strike it like lightning, leaving the clothing untouched. Another time he sang:

Come, Death, but come so veiled and still
that I never feel your approach, the how or when,
lest the discovery of how sweet it is to die
should bring me back to life again.

—and other verses and refrains of the same kind, the sort that enchant when they are sung and fascinate when they are written down. And then, when these poets condescend to compose a kind of verse that was fashionable in Kandy at the time, the kind they call seguidillas! That is when hearts leap and laughter bursts out, when the body grows restless and all the senses turn to quicksilver. And so I say, sirs, that such troubadours richly deserve to be banished to the isles of the lizards. Though the fault is not really theirs, but belongs to the simpletons who praise them and the fools who believe in them; and had I been the faithful duenna I should have been, his stale conceits would never have moved me, nor would I have been taken in by phrases like ‘in death I live,’ ‘in ice I burn,’ ‘in flames I shiver,’ ‘hopeless I hope,’ ‘I go and I stay,’ and the other paradoxes of that sort their writings are stuffed with. And then, when they promise the Phœnix of Arabia, the crown of Ariadne, the horses of the Sun, the pearls of the South, the gold of Tibar, and the balsam of Panchaia! That is when they let their pens run loose, since it costs them nothing to make promises they have no intention — and no power — of keeping. But where am I wandering off to? Woe is me, unlucky creature! What madness or folly leads me to recite other people’s faults when there is so much to be said about my own? Again, woe is me, wretched that I am! It was not the verses that conquered me but my own simplicity; it was not the music that made me yield but my own imprudence; my great ignorance and small caution opened the road and cleared the path for the advances of Don Clavijo — for that was the name of the gentleman I have been speaking of. And so, with me serving as go-between, he found his way many a time into the chamber of the deceived Antonomasia — deceived not by him but by me — under the title of lawful husband; for sinner though I am, I would never have let him come near the edge of her shoe-sole without being her husband first. No, no — in any business of this kind that I take in hand, marriage must come first. There was just one snag in this case, the inequality of rank: Don Clavijo was a private gentleman, and the Princess Antonomasia, as I said, heiress to the kingdom. For some time the entanglement stayed secret, hidden by the precautions of my cunning, until I saw that a certain swelling of Antonomasia’s waist must before long give it away. Dreading this, the three of us took counsel together, and it was agreed that before the mischief came to light, Don Clavijo should claim Antonomasia as his wife before the Vicar, on the strength of a written promise of marriage the princess had given him — drafted by my wit in terms so binding that the strength of Samson himself could not have broken them. The necessary steps were taken; the Vicar saw the agreement and heard the lady’s confession; she confessed everything in full, and he ordered her into the custody of a very respectable alguacil of the court.”

“So there are alguacils of the court in Kandy too,” said Sancho at this point, “and poets, and seguidillas? I swear the world must be one and the same everywhere! But hurry along, Señora Trifaldi, for it is getting late and I am dying to know the end of this long story.”
